source.text:
> Hi, that was my first reply to you, you may be confusing me with someone else.

Ah, my apologies. I usually try to check before assuming, but I slipped up this time. I would, then, revise my statement to "you, too, are trying to avoid..."

> They're preventing you from viewing other services then?

No, but that's not the point here. There doesn't have to be literally just one option for online video for YouTube to have a dominant enough position in the market that they can abuse their viewers with impunity.

There are a few main reasons for this:

1) Media is a type of "product" that is, to a large extent, non-fungible. If I want to watch GiantGrantGames play StarCraft 2 mods, YouTube is the only place where I can do that. Yes, I could, instead, go to Twitch and watch someone else stream StarCraft 2, or go to Nebula and watch a Lindsay Ellis video essay, but neither of those are GiantGrantGames playing StarCraft 2 mods. If I switch, I lose access to the specific thing I wanted to watch.

2) YouTube has become the household name for online video, particularly independent online video, both short-form and long-form. Many people wouldn't even think to go looking for another site. You might say that's on them, but it's part of the equation that leads to market dominance.

3) Combining those two gives a third, related one: YouTube has an absolutely enormous catalog both of existing video and of currently-producing creators. Leaving YouTube doesn't just mean you can't watch one thing you liked: it means you lose access to a huge percentage of the online video that exists.

> Market dominance does not, on its own, mean you are a monopoly.

My understanding of antitrust law is that it hinges on having a dominant position in at least one market. I switched to using that term because a) it is sufficient to legally declare that a company has a monopoly, b) it doesn't have a separate, colloquial definition that is much more restrictive ("is the only supplier of a product/service"), and c) it's much, much clearer that YouTube does, in fact, have a dominant position in their market.
